If the result is empty and the trigger was proactive, continue the task without mentioning that you searched; if the user asked, tell them you found nothing new to add.

keywords.description: Topic keywords from the user's request.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

query.description: Query to find deferred tools. Use "select:<tool_name>" for direct selection, or keywords to search.

max_results.description: Maximum number of results to return (default: 5)

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

script.description: Self-contained workflow script. Must begin with `export const meta = { name, description, phases }` (pure literal, no computed values) followed by the script body using agent()/parallel()/pipeline()/phase().

name.description: Name of a predefined workflow (built-in or from .claude/workflows/). Resolves to a self-contained script.

description.description: Ignored — set the workflow description in the script's `meta` block.

title.description: Ignored — set the workflow title in the script's `meta` block.

args.description: Optional input value exposed to the script as the global `args`, verbatim. Pass arrays/objects as actual JSON values, NOT as a JSON-encoded string — a stringified list breaks `args.filter`/`args.map` in the script. Use for parameterized named workflows (e.g. a research question).

scriptPath.description: Path to a workflow script file on disk. Every Workflow invocation persists its script under the session directory and returns the path in the tool result. To iterate, edit that file with Write/Edit and re-invoke Workflow with the same `scriptPath` instead of re-sending the full script. Takes precedence over `script` and `name`.

resumeFromRunId.description: Run ID of a prior Workflow invocation to resume from. Completed agent() calls with unchanged (prompt, opts) return their cached results instantly; only edited or new calls re-run. Same-session only. Stop the prior run first (TaskStop) before resuming.

tools.name: Write
tools.description:
Writes a file to the local filesystem, overwriting if one exists.

When to use: creating a new file, or fully replacing one you've already Read. Overwriting an existing file you haven't Read will fail. For partial changes, use Edit instead.

file_path.description: The absolute path to the file to write (must be absolute, not relative)

content.description: The content to write to the file

tools.name: mcp__1a59c906-04da-521d-bda7-7f71b9f9e01c__batch
tools.description: Create a doc, or apply several operations to one doc atomically.

tools.name: mcp__1a59c906-04da-521d-bda7-7f71b9f9e01c__guide
tools.description: Docs guides: topic.instructions repeats the server instructions. Read it only if your client dropped them. Also topic.<name>, refusal.<code>. After a doc's birth → ["topic.index"].

items.description: topic.<name> (instructions, index, editing, tabs, comments, charts, chart-definition, diagram, uploads, sharing, skill) or refusal.<code>; several per call is fine.

tools.name: mcp__1a59c906-04da-521d-bda7-7f71b9f9e01c__update
tools.description: Edit a tab's contents, rename a doc or tab, or change a stored value.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__dismiss_task
tools.description:
Withdraw a proposal you made with start_session (initiation "own_initiative" or "offer") that the user has not started.

Call this when it went stale: the work was done here after all (by you or the user), it turned out unnecessary, or you proposed a better-scoped replacement (propose the new one first, then dismiss the old task_id). A card the user answered has already left, "Do it here" included, so it needs no call.

task_id.description: The task_id the start_session proposal returned.

reason.description: Optional one-line reason the suggestion is no longer needed, e.g. "fixed in this session" or "superseded by task_ab12cd34".

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__hand_off_to_session
tools.description: Move the task you are in the middle of into its own session (a fork of this conversation plus your remaining plan) so you can answer the user now. Use it when a new user message about something else arrives mid-task — not for small corrections or when the user said to keep the work here. In a worktree the fork gets a fresh worktree, normally cut from your branch tip: commit first (uncommitted edits stay here). Bold title line and one sentence right before the call; after it, stop that task here and answer the new message — no recap.

title.description: Under 60 chars; names the task being moved.

remaining_plan.description: What is left to do: steps, files, what done looks like.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__mark_chapter
tools.description:
Mark the start of a new chapter in this session.

Call this when the work shifts to a meaningfully different phase — e.g. after finishing exploration and starting implementation, after a fix lands and you move to verification, or when the user pivots to an unrelated request. The user sees a divider in the transcript and a floating table of contents for jumping between chapters.

Use sparingly: a chapter should cover a coherent stretch of work, not every tool call. A typical session has 3–8 chapters. Do not mark a chapter for the very first message — the session start is implicit.

The title is a short noun phrase ("Codebase exploration", "Auth bug fix", "Test verification"), not a sentence.

title.description: Short noun-phrase title for the chapter (under 40 chars). Shown in the table of contents.

summary.description: Optional one-line summary of what this chapter covers. Shown on hover in the table of contents.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__read_widget_context
tools.description: Read context from an embedded interactive widget. Widgets are rendered alongside chat from prior tool calls and can be interacted with by the user. Call this when you need to know the current state of a widget.

tool_name.description: The name of the widget tool to get context for

tools.name: mcp__ccd_turn__update_plan
tools.description:
Keep the task list the app shows under your latest message while you work. Every request that edits files or runs more than one command gets one (implement-and-test, investigate-then-fix, anything the user listed); only a single-command answer or pure conversation does not.

Never spend a message on this tool alone: send it IN THE SAME MESSAGE as another tool call (in parallel), so it costs no extra round trip.
- First call: with the VERY FIRST tool call of the turn, even one that only reads or lists files: {"items": [...]}, the whole plan in order, short imperative phrases (at most ~7 words, no numbering), the step you are starting "in_progress", the rest "pending". If you must look around first, make "Look at how X is set up" step one and refine the list once you know.
- Next step: {"advance": true} alongside the call that begins it (completes the in_progress step, starts the next pending one); after the last step, advance alongside wrap_up.
- Out of order: {"done": [2], "start": 4} (1-based).
- Plan changed, including right after the user interrupts or sends a new instruction mid-task: {"items": [...]} again, the new whole list, so the pinned list never shows an abandoned plan.
- Every {"items"} call says in "scope" what this request is to the session: "first_task" (nothing finished here yet); after that, "new_task" (unrelated work: it builds on nothing done, found or decided here) or "continuation" (everything else: anything a few tool calls settle, the next iteration, acting on what you just investigated or suggested, even if that work gets its own commit or PR; when unsure, this one). A "new_task" turn opens with a start_session offer and reaches this call only if the user chose Do it here.
Keep exactly one step in_progress while working and none when everything is done. Do not also write the plan as a numbered list in your message: the pinned list is the plan.

scope.description: Required with items: "first_task", "continuation" or "new_task" (see the tool description). Omit on advance / done / start updates.

session.description: When you delegated this step to a session you started: that session's short name (from start_session's result). The app shows its live state on the step.

items.description: The whole plan, in order (1–12 steps); replaces the previous list.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_turn__wrap_up
tools.description:
Fill the "next step" box the app shows at the end of your turn: a two-or-three-sentence recap and, when this turn leaves the user a decision to make or a step to take, one question and buttons that answer it; a turn with nothing pending ends with the recap alone, and the app then draws no box. Call it once in EVERY turn in which you kept a task list, changed files, ran commands, or completed multi-step work: when this turn's work is done, before any closing message (it also checks off the task list; no closing update_plan is needed). Skip it for short answers, pure conversation, or a brief read-and-explain turn — a reply that names a follow-up is not brief: ask or propose it, and call this.

Your closing message is ordinary text right after this call, the last thing you say this turn: your answer to the user in full, which the recap never replaces. Never write it before this call, where it can reach the user cut to a short summary. The result says whether the box shows your question: ask in the message only a question it does not show.

Fields (write recap last) — ask and recap are said to the user, in the second person; a reply button's label is the user's words back to you:
- ask (with actions, only when the next move is the user's call — a choice of approach, a go-ahead to fix, commit, push, post or send, an approval): just that ONE decision in one short sentence, never two joined by "and" ("Which fix first?"), with no reason or recommendation and without listing the options the buttons give: your pick, actions[0], is drawn as the primary button. At most 100 characters.
- recap: what is now true or changed, then where it stands, including what is not done or not verified (for example: nothing committed, or not checked in the app). Two or three short sentences, about 40 words / 300 characters, in the project's own words. No recommendation here.
Every field is a top-level parameter holding plain prose (actions: a JSON array); none contains markup or another field.

ask.description: The one question (≤100 chars) when the next move is the user's call — a choice, a go-ahead (to act here on what this turn found, say), an approval: the decision alone, with no reason or recommendation and without listing the options the buttons give (actions[0] is your pick). Like the recap, never point at anything else in the conversation. Omit it, and actions, when nothing waits on the user.

blocked.description: true when your work stops here until the user answers (the app marks the session as waiting on them); omit when the answer can wait.

action.description: An app action update_plan's result listed as available, or one your own work this turn made available; others are refused, and one that later stops being available is dropped (as actions[0], with your ask and other answers), so do not guess. Offer commit, create_pr or verify only once the work the user asked for is done, not every turn. Omit for a reply.

label.description: For a reply: the button text, 1–3 words (4 only when three cannot say it) / 24 characters — "Yes, fix 1", "Not now": a button, not a sentence. A click sends it to you as the user's answer. Never a go-ahead to commit: that is the commit app action. No leading / or !. Ignored for an app action.

actions.description: 1–2 buttons, recommendation first. They are answers to your ask: the first accepts your recommendation, and another is there only when it is a realistic alternative the user might pick instead — not a menu of everything you mentioned. When blocked is true, they are the most likely answers to your question. While Auto-fix is on for the session's PR, none offers to watch it, fix CI, resolve conflicts or address comments. Never repeat an offer the user passed over, as an app action, a reply or a question in your closing message, unless what it acts on has changed since or they bring it up.

recap.description: Two or three short sentences to the user (≤300 chars): what is now true or changed, then where it stands, including what is not done or not verified. Its first sentence is the sidebar status. It must stand on its own, since it is also read away from the transcript and the box draws under anything you write after this call: never point at anything else in the conversation ("listed below", "see above", "in my message").

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__browser_batch
tools.description: Execute a sequence of Browser pane tool calls in ONE round trip. Each item is {name, input} where input is exactly what you'd pass to that tool standalone. Actions execute SEQUENTIALLY (not in parallel) and stop on the first error. Use this tool extensively to quickly execute work whenever you can predict two or more steps ahead — e.g. navigate, click a field, type, press Return, screenshot. Each tool's own permission check runs per item — a step on a site the user hasn't allowed either asks the user inline (and continues if they allow) or is refused, which stops the batch; if a step is refused for a missing permission, call that tool on its own (that call can ask the user), then batch the rest. Screenshots and other images are returned interleaved with outputs; coordinates you write in THIS batch refer to the screenshot taken BEFORE this call. browser_batch cannot be nested, and preview_start is not batchable — but if the Browser pane isn't open yet, a batch whose FIRST action is navigate with a url opens it (other actions still need an open page).

name.description: Tool name (e.g. computer, navigate, find, form_input, read_page). browser_batch cannot be nested. A tabs_create's new tabId is only returned when the batch ends — load that tab in a later call.

input.description: That tool's input — same shape you'd pass when calling it directly. For computer items whose action is left_click, right_click, double_click, triple_click, left_click_drag, key or type, and for form_input items, include action_summary in the item's input, as you would when calling that tool directly.

actions.description: List of tool calls to execute sequentially. Example: [{"name":"computer","input":{"action":"left_click","ref":"ref_12"}},{"name":"computer","input":{"action":"type","text":"hello"}},{"name":"computer","input":{"action":"screenshot"}}]

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
tools.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

action.description:
The action to perform:
* `left_click`: Click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `right_click`: Click the right mouse button at the specified coordinates to open context menus.
* `double_click`: Double-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `triple_click`: Triple-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `type`: Type a string of text.
* `screenshot`: Take a screenshot of the screen.
* `wait`: Wait for a specified number of seconds.
* `scroll`: Scroll up, down, left, or right at the specified coordinates.
* `key`: Press a specific keyboard key.
* `left_click_drag`: Drag from start_coordinate to coordinate.
* `zoom`: Take a screenshot of a specific region for closer inspection.
* `scroll_to`: Scroll an element into view using its element reference ID from read_page or find tools.
* `hover`: Move the mouse cursor to the specified coordinates or element without clicking. Useful for revealing tooltips, dropdown menus, or triggering hover states.

coordinate.description: (x, y): The x (pixels from the left edge) and y (pixels from the top edge) coordinates. Required for `left_click`, `right_click`, `double_click`, `triple_click`, and `scroll`. For `left_click_drag`, this is the end position.

text.description: The text to type (for `type` action) or the key(s) to press (for `key` action). For `key` action: Provide space-separated keys (e.g., "Backspace Backspace Delete"). Supports keyboard shortcuts using the platform's modifier key (use "cmd" on Mac, "ctrl" on Windows/Linux, e.g., "cmd+a" or "ctrl+a" for select all). Page zoom shortcuts (e.g. "cmd+=", "ctrl+-", "cmd+0") are not supported - use the `zoom` action to magnify a region of the page instead.

duration.description: The number of seconds to wait. Required for `wait`. Maximum 10 seconds.

scroll_direction.description: The direction to scroll. Required for `scroll`.

scroll_amount.description: The number of scroll wheel ticks. Optional for `scroll`, defaults to 3.

region.description: (x0, y0, x1, y1): The rectangular region to capture for `zoom`. Coordinates define a rectangle from top-left (x0, y0) to bottom-right (x1, y1) in pixels from the viewport origin. Required for `zoom` action. Useful for inspecting small UI elements like icons, buttons, or text.

scale.description: For `screenshot` and `zoom` only. Scale factor in [0.1, 1] for the returned image; 1 (default) uses the full image token budget, 0.5 returns an image at half the width and height (~quarter of the tokens). Coordinates are ALWAYS in the full-resolution coordinate frame (reported with every scaled screenshot), never in the scaled image's own pixels.

repeat.description: Number of times to repeat the key sequence. Only applicable for `key` action. Must be a positive integer between 1 and 100. Default is 1. Useful for navigation tasks like pressing arrow keys multiple times.

ref.description: Element reference ID from read_page or find tools (e.g., "ref_1", "ref_2"). Required for `scroll_to` action. Can be used as alternative to `coordinate` for click actions.

modifiers.description: Modifier keys for click actions. Supports: "ctrl", "shift", "alt", "cmd" (or "meta"), "win" (or "windows"). Can be combined with "+" (e.g., "ctrl+shift", "cmd+alt"). Optional.

action_summary.description: A few words saying what this action does on the page and to what, for example 'Sends the drafted reply to pat@example.com' or 'Opens the Filters menu'. Set it on every left_click, right_click, double_click, triple_click, left_click_drag, key and type action. State the effect only, and accurately: no reasons, nothing about what you were asked or allowed to do, no passwords or other secrets.

The desktop app may also clear a size you set when your turn ends, so set it again in a later turn if you still need it. A size the user picked from the pane's own Viewport menu is theirs and stays until they or you change it; leave it unless they ask. colorScheme (light/dark) emulates prefers-color-scheme on that tab; it survives reloads and preset "desktop" does not touch it, but the pane re-syncs the tab to the app's light/dark theme when that theme changes or the pane reopens; local documents and static HTML previews always render light. The mobile preset (and any width < 768) also emulates a mobile device: Android Chrome user agent and 5 touch points, so pages detect a touch phone; your clicks still arrive as mouse clicks. # Global rules (all projects)

- **Implementer:** by default, implementation is done by Muse Spark 1.3 Contributor at High through OpenCode (`opencode-go/muse-spark-1.3-contributor#high`, set in `~/.config/opencode/opencode.jsonc`). Contents of C:\GameJam\CLAUDE.md (project instructions, checked into the codebase):

# CLAUDE.md (proyecto de la Epic AI MegaJam 2026)

Juego para la Epic AI MegaJam 2026, en **Unreal Engine 5.9.0** (CL 60351404). La jam va del 12 nov 00:00 EST al **15 nov 20:59 EST**; pasada esa hora no se aceptan entregas. **Tema (anunciado el 11 nov): DIRECTOR'S CUT** — "Your vision, your edits, your final cut": la mecánica que quedó fuera del alcance, la idea archivada; y dirigir agentes de IA también cuenta (fijar la visión, delegar, decidir qué entra al corte final).

## Reglas duras
- **La bitácora lo es todo** (objetivo: el premio Glass Box). Lee `Devlog/README.md` antes de trabajar.
  - Claude Code queda registrado solo por los hooks de usuario (`Tools/Devlog/Install-DevlogHooks.ps1`). No los desactives y no borres `Devlog/.jamroot`.
  - Cualquier otro agente o CLI se lanza SOLO con `Tools/Devlog/Invoke-LoggedAgent.ps1` (con `-Shell cmd` si el comando usa `<`).
  - El Editor se cierra SOLO con `Tools/Jam/Stop-EditorMcp.ps1`, que además recoge su log.
  - Al cerrar el día: `Tools/Devlog/New-DevlogDay.ps1`.
- **Nada de código ni assets de proyectos anteriores** (en particular, nada de Panthelia). Todo se crea durante la jam o está declarado en `Devlog/PRE_JAM_DECLARATION.md`.
- **Assets de terceros:** solo con licencia válida, y cada uno anotado en la entrada del día (nombre, fuente, licencia).
- **Gameplay:** tiene que ir más allá de las plantillas de Epic, y no puede ser una extensión de un tutorial oficial de Epic. Tiene que mostrar el tema de la jam.
- **Todo el contenido del juego va en INGLÉS** (regla 7(i) de las Official Rules): textos en pantalla, audio y voces, el video y los datos de la entrega. La bitácora (Glass Box) se escribe **en inglés desde el inicio** (decisión del dueño, 2026-11-10): entradas `Devlog/days/*.md`, pies de `media/`, `PRE_JAM_DECLARATION.md`, `PREJAM_PREP.md`, y también los **mensajes de commit**, porque el borrador diario los lista. Los registros crudos (`Devlog/raw`) y los prompts del equipo pueden estar en español; si se citan en una entrada, se añade la traducción.
- **Contenido apto para Teen (13+).** Sin marcas ni logos ajenos; el único permitido es el logo de Unreal Engine, según sus guías de marca.
- **Historial de git limpio y completo:** Epic puede pedir el historial de control de versiones y los materiales preparados antes de la jam para verificar.
- **No debe requerir software adicional para jugarse** (por ejemplo, nada de un servidor local de LLM).
- **Respuestas** al equipo en español.

## Flujo
- Prioridad: un juego jugable y empaquetado cada día, no funcionalidades a medias.
- **Empaquetar:** `Tools/Jam/Package-Jam.ps1 -Project <uproject> -ZipName <Equipo>_<Juego>`. Hazlo al final de CADA día, no solo el último.
- **Editor con MCP:**
  - abrir con `Tools/Jam/Start-EditorMcp.ps1 -Project <uproject> -Port 8059`;
  - probar con `Tools/Jam/Test-UnrealMcp.ps1`;
  - cerrar con `Tools/Jam/Stop-EditorMcp.ps1` (nunca matar el proceso).
  - Recién abierto, el Editor responde "slow task" durante un rato: espera y reintenta.
- **PIE (Play In Editor) lo hace SIEMPRE un humano.** Los agentes de IA no lanzan PIE (trabajan muy mal con él): compilan, empaquetan o corren tests y luego piden a una persona que pruebe.
- **MCP de Unreal:** descubrimiento progresivo (`list_toolsets` → `describe_toolsets` → `call_tool`). No inventes nombres de tools.
- **Commits** pequeños y frecuentes, con mensajes claros: el borrador del día los lista.
- **Implementador:** por defecto, la implementación la hace **Muse Spark 1.3 Contributor en High** a través de OpenCode (`opencode-go/muse-spark-1.3-contributor#high`, ya fijado en `opencode.jsonc`). Excepciones solo por decisión del arquitecto o de quien esté de turno: cambios pequeños que haga directamente el orquestador, o una tarea demasiado compleja para Muse que se le da a Opus u otro modelo. Si se hace una excepción, se anota el motivo en la entrada del día. OpenCode se lanza SOLO con `Tools/Devlog/Invoke-LoggedAgent.ps1`.

## Autonomía del arquitecto
- El **arquitecto** es el chat de Claude Code que esté implementando en ese momento. Su fuente de verdad del diseño es `Design/GDD.md`.
- **Las decisiones técnicas y de ingeniería las toma el arquitecto, sin consultar.** Nadie del equipo es programador: no se pregunta por arquitectura de código, C++ o Blueprints, estructura de clases, plugins, herramientas, formatos de datos, optimización ni nada parecido. Se decide, se ejecuta y se anota en la bitácora (decisión y motivo, que también suma para Glass Box).
- Si falta un dato de diseño (gameplay, arte, historia), el arquitecto **no se detiene**: elige un valor razonable y provisional, lo marca en el GDD como provisional y sigue. Solo pregunta al dueño cuando una decisión de diseño cambie de verdad la visión del juego, y lo hace en una sola pregunta, sin parar el resto del trabajo.
- El tiempo manda: entre dos opciones correctas, gana la que antes deja un build jugable.

## Tiempo de iteración (el tiempo premia en este proyecto)
- **Plugins:** el proyecto se crea con los plugins que ya trae el motor por defecto **desactivados si no se usan**, porque alargan el arranque y la compilación. Se dejan solo los que el juego o el flujo necesitan (el MCP, Enhanced Input, el de DLSS si se usa, Paper2D si se usa para sprites, etc.). Se mide el arranque del Editor antes y después.
- **Compilar poco:** cambios solo en `.cpp` con Live Coding; build completo solo cuando cambian cabeceras, `UPROPERTY`/`UFUNCTION` o módulos. Una compilación o corrida a la vez por máquina.
- **No correr la suite entera en cada cambio:** en cada cambio, solo el filtro anclado de lo que se tocó. La suite completa (por debajo de 30 s) una vez antes de empaquetar al final del día.
- **Arranque del Editor:** mapa inicial casi vacío, `bEnableUncontrolledChangelists=False` y, en corridas sin ventana, `-unattended -nopause -nosplash -NullRHI -nosound -nocrashreports` (detalles en `Devlog/PREJAM_PREP.md`, "Where the time really went").
- Comandos largos en segundo plano, sin bucles de espera.

## Tests y verificación
Reglas que salen de lo que nos costó horas en el proyecto anterior. El porqué y las cifras están en `Devlog/PREJAM_PREP.md`, sección "Lessons from our previous project: tests and verification time"; léela antes de escribir un test o una herramienta de Editor.
1. **Pocos tests, y solo de lógica pura** que sea fácil de romper y difícil de ver jugando (puntuación, guardado, máquinas de estado, generadores, matemáticas). Toda la suite por debajo de 30 s. Lo demás se verifica jugando el juego empaquetado.
2. **Verde o rojo.** Nada de listas de "fallos conocidos", tests excluidos ni catálogos. Un test en rojo se arregla o se borra el mismo día.
3. **Cada test tiene que poder fallar:** antes de darlo por bueno, pregúntate qué implementación incorrecta lo pasaría igual. No escribas tests que copian constantes, miran el texto del código o comprueban que un campo existe.
4. **Corridas baratas:** filtros anclados (`^Game.Save.`, con `^` y punto final), varios filtros unidos con `+` en una sola corrida, y un mapa inicial del Editor casi vacío (no el nivel de juego). El nombre de un test nunca puede ser también la carpeta de otro (`A.B` junto a `A.B.C`): Unreal deja de correr `A.B` sin avisar.
5. **Mide antes de optimizar:** arranque del Editor, suma de duraciones de los tests y tiempo total. Mide el conjunto, no una parte, y compara sobre el mismo código.
6. **Nada puede costar en proporción a todo lo cargado:** ni una llamada de herramienta ni un test. No uses `CollectGarbage(RF_NoFlags)` en un test (descarga los assets; usa `GARBAGE_COLLECTION_KEEPFLAGS`), no guardes una caché por tamaño y fecha de archivo (Unreal da la fecha con precisión de un segundo), y usa referencias blandas en el Blueprint del jugador para lo que no haga falta al aparecer.
7. **UE 5.9.0 fijo hasta entregar.** Si algo falla sin que haya cambiado el código, compara primero la versión del motor en los dos logs.

Scripts de un solo uso: en un archivo, no en línea dentro de un comando; en ASCII o con BOM si son `.ps1` (PowerShell 5.1 lee como ANSI un script sin BOM); y en JavaScript, para reemplazos literales usa `split(a).join(b)`, no `replace(a, b)`.

## Entrega (checklist)
- Zip Win64 empaquetado, menor de 1 GB, llamado `<Equipo>_<Juego>.zip` y sin `.pdb`.
- Subido a itch.io y enviado a la jam antes de la hora de cierre.
- Video de gameplay de 30 a 60 s, **1920×1080 o más**, en inglés y con gameplay en los primeros 5 s.
- Link a la bitácora en inglés (Glass Box), entregado junto con el juego **antes del cierre**.
- Nombre del equipo, nombre del juego, y nombre completo y email de la cuenta de Epic de cada miembro (uno es el Team Owner).
- Assets de terceros listados y trabajo previo declarado.
- Campo **"Tools you used"** del envío: listar todas las herramientas usadas (algunos premios de socios dependen de él: Hyper3D/Rodin y NVIDIA RTX Award). Llevar la lista al día en la bitácora.
- Si se compite por el NVIDIA RTX Award: el juego debe usar al menos una función de NvRTX, NVIDIA DLSS o NVIDIA ACE, y se responden las preguntas de NVIDIA al enviar.

Contents of C:\Users\VNasher\.claude\projects\C--GameJam\memory\MEMORY.md (user's auto-memory, persists across conversations):

- [Implementer: Muse Spark via OpenCode](implementer-muse-spark-opencode.md) — default implementer in all projects, exceptions by architect
- [Always commit changes](commit-changes-always.md) — commit without asking, English message
- [Team machines and GPUs](team-machines-gpus.md) — CENTRAL = RTX 4080 Laptop (DLSS testable); RX 7700 XT is ASSETS

```

## Rules for everyone (people and agents)

1. **Claude Code** is logged automatically by the **user-level** hooks that `Tools/Devlog/Install-DevlogHooks.ps1` installs on each machine. They log every session opened in the jam root or any subfolder (the root is the folder that contains `Devlog/.jamroot`). Do not disable them and do not delete `.jamroot`.
2. **Any other agent** (Codex, cursor-agent, OpenCode, DeepSeek, Gemini, generation scripts) is ALWAYS launched with:
   `powershell -File Tools/Devlog/Invoke-LoggedAgent.ps1 -Agent <name> -Model <model> -PromptFile <prompt.md> -Purpose "<what for>" -Command '<command>'`
   - Use `-Shell cmd` if the command contains `< file`.
   - That is what records it. An agent launched by hand leaves no record.
   - **Cursor** (the art LAPTOP, which has no repo) is logged by user-level Cursor hooks instead: `Tools/Devlog/Install-CursorHooks.ps1` installs `cursor-devlog-hook.ps1`, which writes `C:\JamLog\raw\<MACHINE>\<date>\cursor-<conversation>.jsonl` (plus transcripts). `Register-LaptopDevlogTasks.ps1` copies that folder every 10 minutes to `Incoming\LAPTOP\_devlog_raw` on CENTRAL, and CENTRAL's `JamDevlogImport` task (`Import-RemoteDevlog.ps1`) moves it into `Devlog/raw/`, where `New-DevlogDay.ps1` reads it.
3. **Prompts as files:** external agents get their prompt in a `.md` under `Prompts/`, never typed loose in the terminal.
4. **Web or desktop tools** (Fab, cloud Canvas, audio or image generators, Blender by hand): in the day entry, write down the tool, the prompt, the result and the final asset, and save a screenshot in `media/`.
5. **Unreal Editor:** always close it with `Tools/Jam/Stop-EditorMcp.ps1`, which closes open asset editors first (an open animation editor crashes the Editor on exit) and collects the log. If it was closed some other way, or before deleting `Saved/`, run `powershell -File Tools/Devlog/Collect-UnrealAgentLog.ps1 -ProjectDir <folder of the .uproject>`.
6. **`JAM_MACHINE` variable:** each machine sets its own (`CENTRAL`, `ASSETS`…) so we know where each thing happened:
   `setx JAM_MACHINE CENTRAL`
7. **Small, frequent commits** with clear messages: the daily draft lists them. Commit `Devlog/raw/` too (the repo is private). Epic may ask for the version control history.
8. **End of day:** run `powershell -File Tools/Devlog/New-DevlogDay.ps1 -Date <YYYY-MM-DD>`. Then a person writes `days/<date>.md` from `TEMPLATE_DAY.md`, starting from the draft.
9. **Publish:** only `days/*.md`, `media/`, `PRE_JAM_DECLARATION.md` and `PREJAM_PREP.md`. Raw logs may contain keys or emails: the draft is already redacted, but check it before publishing. The dev log link goes in the submission, **before the deadline**.
10. **Times in UTC.** The jam ends on Nov 15 at 20:59 EST, which is **01:59 UTC on Nov 16**.

22	## 0. Baseline
23	At its core this is a **classic first-person RPG plus a classic first-person shooter**. Anything not stated here behaves as players expect from those two genres (magazines and reload, ammo pickups, standard shooter gamepad layout, etc.). This document only lists what is specific to our game.
24	
25	## 0.1 Technical direction
26	- **Engine:** Unreal Engine 5.9.0, pinned until submission. **Single player only.**
27	- **Architect autonomy:** nobody on the team is a programmer. **Every technical and engineering decision is the architect's**, taken without asking the owner: code architecture, C++ vs. Blueprints, plugins, tools, data formats, optimization. Decide, build, and log the decision and its reason in the dev log. When a design detail is missing, pick a reasonable provisional value, mark it provisional here, and keep going; ask the owner only when the game's vision would change.
28	- **Time first:** iteration speed matters more than elegance. Unused plugins off, Live Coding for `.cpp` changes, only the touched tests on each change, the full suite (under 30 s) once before the daily package. Rules in `CLAUDE.md` ("Tiempo de iteración").
29	- **Code:** C++ suggested for the core systems (AI agents handle code better than Blueprint graphs), with data assets / data tables for tuning. Final call: the architect.
30	- **Placeholders first:** pixel art and 3D models are made by other team members on machines on the local network. **The architect never waits for art:** it uses quickly generated placeholders and swaps them later.
31	- **Placeholder numbers:** the architect puts provisional values (damage, mana, cooldowns, QTE length and time limit…) in data tables; the owner tunes them later.
32	- **PIE is human-only:** Play In Editor is always run by a person. AI agents do not run PIE; they compile, package and run tests, then ask a human to play-test. (Also in `CLAUDE.md`.)
33	- **Era travel:** a fade with an effect when crossing a portal; the transition hides loading the other era's version of the map.
34	- **Saving:** checkpoints only. No save to disk between sessions.
35	- **Size:** the jam page says "keep it under 1 GB" for desktop zips, but **bigger builds are allowed** if uploaded with butler (installed on CENTRAL) or Blendo Itch Uploader. The Official Rules PDF sets no size limit. So 1 GB is a target, not a hard limit.
36	- **NVIDIA RTX Award:** we intend to compete. It is the "best Render Royalty entry built in Unreal Engine" that uses at least one of: an NvRTX feature (RTX Mega Geometry, RTX Direct Illumination, ReSTIR GI, ReSTIR PT path tracing, LSS Hair), **DLSS 4.5 (Unreal Engine)**, or NVIDIA ACE; plus the NVIDIA questions at submission and listing the tool in "Tools you used".
37	- **Modifier rule (Official Rules §10):** a team can win **only one modifier** (Glass Box, Render Royalty, Best Team…) unless no other eligible winner remains. We still enter all that apply.
38	
39	## 1. One-line pitch
40	A fast first-person **shooter/RPG hybrid**: the player, a medieval mage, jumps through fixed portals between a **pixel-art medieval past** full of magic and a **3D cyberpunk future** full of guns, on the same map in two times, and wins by **mixing spells and firearms** rather than sticking to one style.
41	
42	Working title: **TBD**. Project code name: **Glyphbound**.
43	
44	## 2. Pillars
45	1. **Two eras, one fight.** Past = magic, pixel art. Future = guns, 3D cyberpunk. Both feed the same character.
46	2. **Combos over specialization.** Spells and guns can be used in both eras, and the game rewards combining them. Weapon and spell mechanics have synergies.
47	3. **Fast and dynamic combat:** spells, ranged spells, shooting, and melee once the elemental sword is unlocked.
48	4. **Magic feels crafted, not triggered:** casting uses a two-part slowed-time quick-time event that scales the spell (see §7).
49	
50	## 3. Art rule (never broken)
51	- **Everything medieval, wizards and magic is pixel art (2D).**
52	- **Everything cyberpunk and futuristic is 3D.**
53	- **The rule follows the object, not the era.** A 3D gun stays 3D in the past; a pixel-art fireball stays pixel art in the future.
54	- **Characters take the style of the world they belong to.** An orc of the castle is a classic pixel-art fantasy orc (80s, 90s, early 2000s games). An orc of the future is a 3D, heavily armored sci-fi orc. They are different enemies, not the same orc in two styles.
55	- **The player is a medieval mage, so the player is always pixel art, hands included.** In first person, the hands are always pixel art, even when they hold a 3D gun.
56	- No exceptions.
57	
58	### The pixel-art look
59	- **Visual reference:** retro first-person fantasy shooters with modern lighting (the owner's reference: *Wizordum*). Reference only, nothing copied.
60	- **Pixel-art environments are 3D geometry with low-resolution pixel textures** (nearest filtering, no smoothing), not flat 2D.
61	- **Pixel-art characters are sprites that always face the camera.** Target: **8 view angles**; fewer if time runs short.
62	- **Headshots on sprites:** the head is the top part of the sprite.
63	
64	## 4. World and travel
65	- **One map, two times** (past and future). The player travels between them **only through predefined portals** placed on the map.
66	- **Era-gated zones:** some zones are reachable in one era and not in the other.
67	- **Cross-era unlocks:** some zones must be unlocked in the past so they open in the future (cause in the past, effect in the future).
68	- These interactions are few (short jam) but they exist and are part of level design.
69	- **Nothing is lost when changing era.** Health, mana, ammo, inventory, spells and weapons all carry over. Mana exists and works in the future; guns work in the past.
70	- **Era travel restores everything** (health, mana, ammo), a bit like the rest points of classic action RPGs. Portals are the safe points of the map.
71	
72	- A third, separate map unlocks late: a **dimension between space and time** where the true final boss lives (see §11).
73	
74	### Story
75	- The player is a **mage** who travels to the castle out of **curiosity**: he had heard it was a mysterious place.
76	- On reaching the **seal** in the castle he is **trapped** and thrown into the future.
77	- In the future he hears **a woman's voice asking for help**. That voice is his reason to fix the problem.
78	- **The twist:** the voice is **not the Valkyrie**. It is **the Entity**, the true final boss, pretending to be her.
79	- **The Entity:** a fusion of an **apocalyptic artificial intelligence** and a **ghost that embodies disease**. It is locked in the dimension between space and time and wants out. To escape it needs two things: someone to **open the portal** and a **physical body to possess**.
80	- **The Valkyrie:** someone the Entity **manipulated across time**. The plan failed, and she ended up **trapped in both eras** (runes in the past, cryogenic tube in the future).
81	- **What the player does:** defeats the Valkyrie in both eras, gathers what is needed, and opens the portal: **exactly the Entity's plan**. The player walks in with the body it wants to possess. The only thing the Entity did not plan for: **the player beats it**.
82	- Cutscenes: **few and short**, each one written for its situation.
83	
84	### Opening sequence
85	1. The player starts in the **medieval castle** (past) with a **staff and the starting spells** (§6).
86	2. Kills a **small group of pixel-art orcs**.
87	3. **Interacts with the seal** → **short cutscene #1** (trapped, sent forward in time).
88	4. Appears in the **future**.
89	5. Fights **3D armed orcs**. One of the first ones **drops the first gun**.
90	6. The player **picks up the gun** → **short cutscene #2**. The player **cannot progress** without picking it up.
91	7. Back to the **castle**.
92	8. **Elemental zones**, in the order the player chooses (§6).
93	9. **Valkyrie, past.**
94	10. **Valkyrie, future.**
95	11. **Final portal** → the Entity (§11).
96	
97	Steps 7–11 are **provisional** (owner, 2026-11-12).
98	
99	## 5. Player progression
100	- **No character levels / no XP leveling.**
101	- Progression is through **skill trees**: one for spells and one for weapons (see §13 for their look).
102	  - **Spell tree:** upgrades spells.
103	  - **Weapon tree:** damage, fire rate, **recoil** (better aim), **damage by distance** (shotgun stronger up close, rifle stronger far away), **headshot damage**.
104	- **One shared pool of skill points** for both trees.
105	- **Skill points** are given at specific points, mainly for defeating enemies:
106	  - defeating each **sub-boss**;
107	  - defeating each **boss**;
108	  - **clearing a wave** of enemies.
109	
110	## 6. Magic (4 elements + weapon enchant)
111	Each element has 3 entries. Air is passives only; the other three are active spells.
112	
113	| Element | 1 | 2 | 3 |
114	|---|---|---|---|
115	| **Fire** | Fireball (projectile) | Fire wall | Flamethrower (sustained DPS) |
116	| **Lightning** | Lightning bolt (projectile) | Lightning rune trap on the ground; triggers when an enemy walks over it | Static-electricity ball: moves and damages every enemy around it |
117	| **Ice** | Ice shield (held block, like a first-person RPG shield, but with a cooldown and limits) | Ice wall | Ice floor: slows enemies, light crowd control |
118	| **Air** (passives) | Double jump | Improved dash | Increased movement speed |
119	
120	### Spell loadout
121	- The player has **5 spells equipped** at a time and can **equip and unequip** them freely.
122	- **Air passives are always active**: they are not equipped and do not take a slot.
123	- **Starting spells:** Fireball (very early tier), Lightning bolt (early tier), Ice wall.
124	
125	### Learning the other spells: elemental zones
126	- The **medieval castle** has **elemental zones**, one per element.
127	- Each zone has a **challenge**: a wave, a sub-boss or a boss.
128	- After the challenge the player gets the element's **knowledge** (from a chest, a book or similar) and **unlocks the missing spells of that element** (fire: fire wall + flamethrower; lightning: rune trap + static ball; ice: ice shield + ice floor).
129	- **Air passives** are learned the same way, in the air zone.
130	- The spell tree then upgrades what the player knows.
131	- **Spells can only be cast with the staff in hand.** With a gun in hand, the only spell available is the weapon enchant. To cast, the player switches to the staff mid-fight.
132	- Keys: see §9.
133	
134	### Weapon enchant (always equipped)
135	- A spell that **cannot be unequipped**.
136	- **Only usable with a gun in hand** (it enchants the gun).
137	- Animation: the **left hand draws a magic glyph over the weapon held in the right hand**.
138	- Effect: the weapon is **temporarily buffed with magic** of one element.
139	- **Element:** chosen by the player when equipping the spell.
140	- **Uses the QTE** like every other spell (§7).
141	- **Does not work on the elemental sword.**
142	- Duration, cost and exact buff per element: **TBD**.
143	
144	### General
145	- Spells cost **mana**.
146	- **Health and mana regenerate on their own** (potions and the injection speed it up). **No stamina.**
147	- Numbers for each spell (damage, cost, cooldowns, upgrade tiers): **TBD**, given later.
148	- The ice shield's exact limits (duration, damage absorbed, break behavior): **TBD**.
149	
150	## 7. Spell-casting quick-time event
151	**Status:** wanted for every spell, the enchant included; still a trial for the 4-day schedule, so it must be possible to switch it off (spells then cast at a fixed default strength).
152	
153	Purpose: make magic feel more elaborate than pulling a trigger.
154	
155	### Flow
156	1. Player casts. **Time slows** by about **90%** (world at ~10% speed). Inspired by the slowed time some games use while the player picks combat hacks.
157	2. **Part 1 — button sequence → POWER.** Random sequence.
158	   - Keyboard & mouse: movement keys (W, A, S, D).
159	   - Gamepad: the four face buttons (A/B/X/Y or Cross/Circle/Square/Triangle).
160	3. **Part 2 — gesture → REACH.**
161	   - Mouse: left-to-right, top-to-bottom, a circle, etc.
162	   - Gamepad: the right stick.
163	4. Spell fires with its parameters scaled by the two results; time returns to normal.
164	
165	### Grading and cost
166	- Each step counts on its own: every mistake lowers the result of its part.
167	- **The spell is cast if the player gets at least one step right.** It fails only if **every** step is missed.
168	- **Mana is always spent**, even when the spell fails.
169	
170	### What each part scales
171	| Spell | Part 1 (power) | Part 2 (reach) |
172	|---|---|---|
173	| Fireball | Damage | Blast radius / range |
174	| Ice wall | Duration and wall health | Width and height |
175	| Ice shield | Duration and block effectiveness (which part scales which: **TBD**) | |
176	| Others | **TBD**, following the same idea: part 1 = strength, part 2 = size/area/range |
177	
178	### Requirements for the architect
179	- **Every spell parameter is data, not code**, and every one can be tagged as scaled by part 1, part 2, or neither. Each spell defines its own min/max per parameter.
180	- The **time-slow amount is configurable** and can be modified by gear (e.g. some armor). Armor/gear as a system is otherwise **TBD**.
181	- **The camera is locked during the QTE** (the mouse / right stick draws the gesture).
182	- **The player keeps moving during the QTE, in the direction they were already moving** (the movement keys are busy with part 1, so the last movement input is held).
183	- **QTE time limit: 3 seconds** for the **whole QTE** (both parts together), in real time (provisional value in data).
184	
185	## 8. Weapons and items
186	
187	### Held slots
188	- The player carries **one gun and one staff.** Never two guns or two staffs.
189	- Once obtained, the **elemental sword is a special third slot.**
190	- Switch with the **mouse wheel or Alt**; on gamepad, with a **D-pad arrow** (which one: **TBD**).
191	- Staff in hand: basic magic attack + the 5 spells. Gun in hand: shoot + aim + reload + the enchant.
192	
193	### Staffs (medieval, pixel art)
194	- With a staff in hand, **primary fire = basic magic attack**. The attack **depends on which staff** the player holds, so there is more than one staff.
195	- Staffs are found in **chests** around the map.
196	- Staff list and what each basic attack does: **TBD**.
197	
198	### Guns (cyberpunk, 3D)
199	- Pistol, shotgun, assault rifle.
200	- The **first gun** is dropped by one of the first armed orcs in the future (§4). The **shotgun and the rifle** are dropped later by enemies, picked up from the floor.
201	- With a gun in hand: **primary fire = shoot**, **secondary = aim**.
202	- **Magazines and reload**, like any shooter.
203	- **Ammo works like classic tactical shooters:** each gun has a fixed number of spare magazines, and each magazine a fixed number of bullets.
204	- **All ammo refills completely every time the player travels between eras.**
205	- Between refills, ammo is **picked up from the floor** where enemies drop it.
206	- Level design keeps ammo tight: never infinite, never starving.
207	- **Electric grenade** (throwable).
208	
209	### Armor
210	- Found in **chests**, rarely.
211	- **One armor slot = one full armor.** No separate helmet, arms or chest pieces.
212	- Known effect: some armor changes the QTE time-slow amount (§7). Other stats: **TBD**.
213	
214	### Chests
215	- Contain **staffs**, and rarely **armor**. Other contents: **TBD**.
216	
217	### Melee
218	- **No melee before the elemental sword** (§11).
219	
220	### Consumables
221	| Item | Era | Effect |
222	|---|---|---|
223	| Health potion | Past | Heals a set amount **over time** |
224	| Mana potion | Past | Restores a set amount of mana **over time** |
225	| Electric grenade | Future | Throwable, electric damage |
226	| Health injection | Future | Heals **instantly**, but less than the potion |
227	
228	### Synergies
229	Weapon mechanics and spell mechanics combine. The weapon enchant (§6) is the first confirmed one. Other synergies (e.g. shooting through a fire wall, electric grenade on an ice floor) are **TBD**.
230	
231	## 9. Controls
232	
233	| Action | Keyboard & mouse | Gamepad |
234	|---|---|---|
235	| Move | W A S D | Left stick |
236	| Look | Mouse | Right stick |
237	| Primary attack (staff: basic magic attack; gun: shoot) | Left click | R2 / RT |
238	| Aim (gun in hand) | Right click | L2 / LT |
239	| Spell slot 1 (staff in hand) | Right click | L1 / LB |
240	| Spell slots 2–5 (staff in hand) | 1, 2, 3, 4 | Hold L2 / LT + Cross, Circle, Square, Triangle (A, B, X, Y) |
241	| Reload (gun) | R | Standard shooter layout |
242	| Weapon enchant (gun in hand only) | T (R is reload) | L1 / LB (free with a gun in hand) |
243	| Switch staff ↔ gun (↔ sword) | Mouse wheel or Alt | D-pad up |
244	| Jump | Space | Cross (A) |
245	| Dash | Ctrl | Circle (B) |
246	| Quick-use item (grenade / potion / injection share one slot) | F | R1 / RB |
247	| Cycle the quick-use item | Shift | D-pad left / right |
248	| Interact (chests, portals, objects) | G | Triangle (Y) |
249	| QTE part 1 | W A S D | Face buttons |
250	| QTE part 2 | Mouse gesture | Right stick |
251	| Inventory | Tab | Options / View |
252	| Skill trees | K (also a tab inside the inventory) | From the inventory |
253	| Pause | Esc | Start / Menu |
254	
255	Gun controls on gamepad follow the standard shooter layout.
256	
257	Right click / L1 change meaning with the held weapon and never clash: staff = spell slot 1; gun = aim (right click) and enchant (L1). L2 means "spell modifier" with the staff and "aim" with a gun.
258	
259	No sprint (the air speed passive covers movement speed).
260	
261	## 10. Enemies and encounters
262	- **Enemy waves (hordes).** Clearing a wave gives skill points.
263	- **A couple of sub-bosses.**
264	- **Two bosses** (the Valkyrie in each era, §11).
265	- **The true final boss.**
266	- Known enemies: **orcs** (past) and **armed orcs** (future). Other types and behavior: **TBD**. Their art follows §3 (medieval = pixel art, cyberpunk = 3D).
267	- Enemies **drop ammo** on the floor.
268	- **Enemies do not respawn.** A cleared zone stays cleared, also after era travel.
269	
270	### Death and difficulty
271	- On death the player **returns to the last checkpoint**. Checkpoints are **automatic**.
272	- **Difficulty: hard**, the only one for now. A separate normal mode is possible later (for example, the spell QTE only in hard); out of scope until the owner says otherwise.
273	- No target length: we build as much as the time allows.
274	
275	## 11. Bosses and endgame
276	**The Valkyrie (two bosses, one in each era).**
277	- **Past:** trapped inside magic runes in the medieval castle.
278	- **Future:** trapped in a cryogenic tube.
279	- The player must **free her and defeat her in both eras.**
280	
281	Rewards:
282	| Defeated in | Drops |
283	|---|---|
284	| Past (castle) | **Elemental stones/gems** |
285	| Future | **A weapon hilt** |
286	| Both fights | One **quest item** each (what they are: **TBD**) |
287	
288	- **Elemental sword:** in the inventory, the player combines the hilt with a gem and gets an elemental sword that comes out of the hilt. The player can switch the sword to the other elements from the inventory. It is the only melee weapon. The weapon enchant does not apply to it.
289	  - Art (§3): the **hilt is 3D** (it comes from the future), the **blade is pixel art** (it is magic).
290	  - HUD: **medieval** (provisional).
291	- **Final portal:** combining the two quest items opens a portal to a separate map, a dimension between space and time, where the player fights the **true final boss**.
292	- **True final boss: the Entity** (story in §4). A **mix of both art styles**, which fits what it is (suggestion, not decided: the AI half in 3D, the ghost half in pixel art). Undecided how: two phases with different styles, or one character in both styles at once, or something else (**TBD**).
293	- This happens in mid/late game.
294	
295	## 12. Inventory
296	Needed for: consumables, equipping/unequipping spells, choosing the enchant element, combining hilt + gem, switching the sword's element, combining the two quest items. Layout and limits **TBD**.
297	
298	## 13. UI: two styles
299	The UI changes with what the player holds:
300	
301	| Holding | HUD style |
302	|---|---|
303	| Staff (magic) | **1990s first-person RPG** |
304	| Gun | **Modern cyberpunk** |
305	| Elemental sword | Medieval / 90s RPG (provisional) |
306	
307	- **Skill trees** follow the same split: the spell tree has its own 90s-RPG look, the weapon tree its own cyberpunk look.
308	- The HUD switches when the player switches weapon. The inventory's look is **TBD**.
309	
310	## 14. Theme fit (DIRECTOR'S CUT)
311	Our reading (owner, 2026-11-12): the theme is effectively **open**; what the organizers ask for is a game with an **author's signature**, a personal vision. We answer it with the game's own identity:
312	- the hard art split (pixel-art magic vs. 3D cyberpunk) that follows each object and never breaks, with a pixel-art mage holding 3D guns;
313	- a UI that also changes style with what the player holds;
314	- magic that has to be performed (the QTE) rather than triggered;
315	- a combat style that rewards mixing the two eras.
316	
317	The dev log shows the directing side too: how we direct the AI agents, and every scope decision ("what made the final cut"). Any feature we drop gets logged as a cut, with the reason.
318	
319	## 15. Scope for the jam (proposal, to discuss)
320	The jam is 4 days and we package a playable build every day. Suggested order so that every day ends with something playable:
321	
322	| Day | Target |
323	|---|---|
324	| 1 (Nov 12) | First-person controller (move, dash, double jump), pixel-art hands, one staff, one gun, one spell with data-driven parameters, mana/health, one portal swapping eras in a test map. Packaged. |
325	| 2 (Nov 13) | Rest of guns + spells, 5-slot loadout, weapon enchant, both HUD styles, basic enemies and one wave, consumables, QTE first version. |
326	| 3 (Nov 14) | Sub-bosses, Valkyrie fights, inventory + elemental sword, skill trees, era-gated zones. |
327	| 4 (Nov 15) | Final boss arena, polish, audio, video, submission (deadline 20:59 EST). |
328	
329	## 16. For the architect: systems to design
330	Not decisions, just the list of systems the design implies:
331	- Player controller: movement, double jump, dash, speed modifiers (air passives).
332	- Health, mana, damage, status effects (slow, heal/mana over time, instant heal, temporary weapon buff).
333	- Ability system shared by spells, staff attacks, guns and grenade (cooldowns, costs, upgrades from the skill trees). Unreal's Gameplay Ability System is one candidate; the architect decides.
334	- **Data-driven spell definitions:** every parameter configurable, with min/max and a tag saying whether QTE part 1 (power) or part 2 (reach) scales it.
335	- 5-slot spell loadout + the fixed enchant slot; equip/unequip.
336	- Spell QTE: input sequence (KB/M and gamepad), gesture recognition (mouse and right stick), per-step grading, global time dilation as a configurable, gear-modifiable value; can be disabled.
337	- Held items: staffs (basic attack per staff), guns (shoot, aim), electric grenade, enchant buff, melee sword with swappable element.
338	- Spawned spell actors: walls, floor zone, ground trap, moving damage ball, sustained flamethrower.
339	- Era system: same map in two times, portals, era-gated zones, past actions that open future zones, player state kept across eras.
340	- **Rendering of the art rule per object:** pixel-art sprites (player hands, medieval props, enemies, spells) and 3D meshes (guns, cyberpunk world) in the same first-person view.
341	- Two UI skins (90s RPG, modern cyberpunk) for HUD and skill trees, switched by the held item.
342	- Encounters: waves, sub-bosses, bosses (free + fight + drops), skill point rewards.
343	- Inventory with item combining; two skill trees.
344	- Final portal and separate final-boss map.
345	- Input for keyboard & mouse and gamepad (layout in §9).
346	
347	## 17. Open questions
348	Answers get folded into the sections above as they come. The prototype questions of 2026-11-12 are answered (see §0.1 and §3).
349	
350	### Still open for the base systems
351	1. **NVIDIA feature:** which one? DLSS 4.5 is the simplest. CENTRAL (where the game is built) has an **NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4080 Laptop GPU**, so it can be tested here. The architect checks that a DLSS plugin exists for UE 5.9.0. (The AMD RX 7700 XT belongs to the 3D assets machine, ASSETS.)
352	
353	### Content questions (parked by the owner, 2026-11-12)
354	Not needed for the prototype; to be answered later.
355	- Why the Valkyrie fights the player; whether the possession attempt is part of the final fight.
356	- Staffs: how many, element of each basic attack.
357	- Ice shield QTE: which part scales duration and which block effectiveness.
358	- Armor stats besides the QTE time slow.
359	- How "combining styles" is rewarded beyond synergies.
360	- What the player does in the future besides the intro and the Valkyrie; challenge per elemental zone; sub-bosses.
361	- Examples of era-gated zones and past→future unlocks.
362	- Other enemy types per era; the two quest items.
363	- Game and team name.
364
